 by Robert Gandt (Author) Format: Kindle Edition

 SKYGODS is the saga of America's most glamorous airline from its meteoric ascent to its plunge to extinction. Pan Am blazed the way across the world's oceans with its magnificent Clipper ships, launched the first international jet service, was the first to fly the behemoth 747, was the lead customer for America's SST and the Concorde, and was even taking reservations for the first commercial flights to the moon. Told from multiple viewpoints--pilots, stewardesses, management executives--SKYGODS is the life story of an American icon.

The way to think of this book is not so much a history of Pan Am more of a long account of the decline. The early sea plane years are covered a little quickly but that is not the main remit. I had long wanted to read more about why this great airline failed and this book is perfect for that.

It has a well written and interesting narrative, it is easy to read and not too technical which is perfect for a more casual reader. It is written in parts from the perspective of the pilot hence the title.

I would highly recommend it if you just accept that it is not quite a straightforward history of Pan Am.

##### A no-nonsense, novel-like account of Pan Am's 25 year decline.

Reviewed in the United Kingdom on 15 March 2017

Format: Paperback

Verified Purchase

Gandt's no-nonsense, novel-like approach to chronicling Pan Am's rise and catastrophic fall is put to good use here. Following the careers of individual Pan Am fresh hires from the 60's, this book also retains a human touch, with plenty of humour, mischief and sadness (in the case of Lockerbie) mixing in with the corporate tale of woe. The characters in charge of Pan Am are also documented well: Juan Trippe: the pioneering, charming master manipulator, Harold Gray: whose declining medical condition appeared to be an eerie omen for Pan Am's own future of terminal decline, Najeeb Halaby: forced out from the airline he loved, General Seawell: an autocrat by every measure whose gamble of buying National Airlines proved disastrous, Ed Acker: the gung-ho executive whose reign as CEO also proved disappointing as he began selling profitable assets for the company to survive, and finally Tom Plaskett: an apparently nice guy put in charge of nursing a dying patient in its final few years. Throughout, the story is peppered with 'what-ifs': what if Pan Am had been allowed to fly domestic routes from the get-go? What if it had been allowed to merge with TWA, or finally, Northwest? What if the Shah of Iran, of all people, had bought the airline, and what would've happened to America's flag carrier after the Iranian Revolution? The story becomes a sort of epic tragedy, as every time the airline appears to be recovering, uncontrollable events kick it in the gut. The early 70's recession, the 1973 oil crisis, the tragic Lockerbie bombing, and finally, the Gulf War. A good, gripping concise book detailing why the airline that helped launch the jumbo age is no longer with us.
